title: Make It Stick
hook: Friday repair lists turn scattered study tactics into a system memory has to answer to.
counterintuition: A routine can look complete and still fail if it is only one favorite technique. The stronger cycle retrieves, spaces, mixes, checks, repairs, and returns.
tryThisNow: Build a seven-day loop. Add one retrieval slot, one delayed review, one mixed set, one calibration check, and one repair block.
keyTakeaway: Make learning stick with a repeatable loop: retrieve first and space reviews before you mix practice, check confidence, repair misses, and return before confidence coasts.

breakdown.fastRead:
It took Anna one failed practice exam to stop collecting tips. Her semester calendar had beautiful topic blocks, but the question bank proved the old material was gone. On Friday she adds a repair list: missed concepts, delayed retrieval, mixed questions, and one checked explanation.

The pieces now have a rhythm. Retrieval makes memory produce. Spacing makes it recover later. Interleaving trains selection. Calibration checks confidence. Repair turns misses into the next plan.

A system matters because each method protects against a different illusion. Together they keep learning honest after the first week feels familiar.
breakdown.deepRead:
The tiny recorder warms in Manon's palm while she covers her own lines in two scripts and rotates scenes from both roles. She may be called with a few hours notice. Reading the script straight through feels reassuring, but repertory work asks for retrieval, cues, switching, and repair.

Nathan Fuller made the script answer back, line by line, until retrieval had the shape of the stage. As a Guthrie Theater understudy, he covered lines, spoke them from memory, checked accuracy, and later used a palm-sized recorder for other actors' cue lines. The routine mattered because performance would not arrive in page order.

A system is a promise to come back.

Timothy Fellows treated the course like a system: read, question, test, find the hole, and relearn it before the exam did. Reading notes, rhetorical questions during lecture, practice tests, and targeted relearning were not separate tricks. They were parts of a loop that made each week answer to the last one.

That is what synthesis should look like. Not a bag of tips. A calendar with roles for each method, a place where misses go, and a next encounter already scheduled. The loop matters because every piece gives the next piece better evidence.
breakdown.fullRead:
Four colored onboarding folders stretch across the conference table while Michael maps a month for new nurses. The old design gave medication safety in week one, handoff in week two, escalation in week three, and patient education in week four. Clean blocks, clean folders, weak transfer. Floor work will mix all four before lunch. Michael lays out a new schedule: retrieve old content each Monday, simulate mixed handoffs each Thursday, write one repair note on Friday, and revisit misses the next week.

That is the architecture. The learner does not merely meet a topic once and move on. The topic returns after delay, beside another topic, under a different cue, with feedback attached. Each return asks a different question. Can you retrieve it? Can you choose it among neighbors? Can you explain why it fits? Can you spot where your confidence got ahead of performance?

Mary Pat Wenderoth turned a biology course into a rhythm of retrieval, reflection, and visible standards for better answers. Weekly learning paragraphs, Bloom's taxonomy answer keys, and high-structure classes made students work with what they knew, what they missed, and how stronger answers were built. Structure was not a cage. It was a way to keep practice from disappearing into good intentions.

What would your week look like if every miss had a return date?

Farmers Insurance new-agent training does not leave each topic sealed in its own box; the week keeps returning to the same work at a higher level. Training cycles through sales, marketing systems, business planning, and brand advocacy so prior material has to be retrieved and applied in larger contexts. West Point Thayer method is blunt about responsibility: arrive prepared, recite, get checked, and keep moving. Different settings, same pressure on memory to do work before the final test.

Jonas uses that pressure in a bootcamp. "Old material comes back Monday," he tells the cohort while terminal prompts glow on the screens. Every weekly quiz will include last month's commands, and every student will explain one miss in a learning paragraph. The quiz is not a trap. It is a scheduled return. The paragraph makes the miss speak clearly enough to repair.

Chiara builds a small version at lunch, a shoe box of mixed client cards on the counter beside a wrong-answer sheet. Licensing material is too broad for one heroic Saturday. She rotates product questions, regulations, and client scenarios through lunch breaks and Saturday review. Wrong answers do not vanish into shame. They get written down, repaired, and returned to the box.

Lin finds the same pattern in maintenance after the only trained technician is off shift and a fault diagnosis stalls. The postmortem redesigns cross-training around retrieval, simulation, rotating fault types, and repair before certification. A one-time workshop had created attendance. A system creates availability.

Build the loop small enough to repeat. One retrieval slot. One delayed return. One mixed set. One calibration check. One repair block. Then let the week ask again.

examples.title: Anna Builds a Friday Repair List for Comps

planSpec.domain: Anna, a graduate student building a semester study cycle
planSpec.audience: students who have learned the pieces but need a schedule
planSpec.stakes: comps require material from months apart, not last week only
planSpec.requiredBeat: show her moving from topic-by-topic notes to a calendar that returns to old material, mixes questions, checks misses, and repairs weak areas each Friday

examples.scenario: It took Anna one failed practice exam to stop collecting tips. Before, her semester calendar moved topic by topic and her question bank sat untouched until Sunday nights. After, the calendar sends old material back every Wednesday, mixes questions on Thursday, and leaves Friday for a repair list. The missed concepts no longer float around as guilt. Each one has a return date.
examples.whatToDo: Put delayed retrieval, mixed questions, a cue-free check, and a Friday repair list on the semester calendar.
examples.whyItMatters: Comps pull from months at once. Anna needs a system that keeps old material returning, not another tip that works only during the week it is learned.

examples.title: Michael Rebuilds Onboarding Around Recurring Handoffs

planSpec.domain: Michael, a hospital educator designing nurse onboarding
planSpec.audience: trainers who must turn principles into a course architecture
planSpec.stakes: new nurses need transfer from classroom to floor handoffs
planSpec.requiredBeat: he lays out a month that cycles medication safety, handoff, escalation, and patient education through retrieval and simulation instead of one-week blocks

examples.scenario: Four colored onboarding folders stretch across the conference table while Michael studies the simulation schedule and a handoff rubric. The old month has one topic per week. The floor will not. A new nurse may handle medication safety, patient education, and escalation in one hour. Michael's marker pauses above the calendar. He must choose between tidy one-week blocks and a cycle that keeps old topics returning inside mixed simulations.
examples.whatToDo: Cycle medication safety, handoff, escalation, and patient education through weekly retrieval and mixed simulation instead of sealing each topic inside one week.
examples.whyItMatters: Floor transfer requires combined action. Returning topics in mixed simulations trains nurses to retrieve and choose when real handoffs blur the folders.

examples.title: Manon Makes Two Scripts Answer Back

planSpec.domain: Manon, an actor understudying two roles in repertory
planSpec.audience: performers needing retrieval, cues, and interleaving
planSpec.stakes: she may be called in with a few hours notice
planSpec.requiredBeat: she records cue lines, covers her own lines, rotates scenes from both roles, and checks missed entrances before rehearsal

examples.scenario: At 6:05 p.m. in rehearsal room B, the tiny recorder warms in Manon's palm while her covered script lies open on a chair. She records cue lines from both roles, rotates scenes on a handwritten list, and speaks only when the other character's line gives her the opening. One entrance disappears. Before rehearsal, she must choose whether to reread the whole scene or mark that entrance for a delayed cue check.
examples.whatToDo: Use the recorder for cue lines, cover her own lines, rotate scenes from both roles, and schedule missed entrances for a later check.
examples.whyItMatters: Understudy work arrives out of order. Manon needs retrieval shaped by cues and interleaving, not comfort from reading pages straight through.

examples.title: Jonas Brings Last Month Back on Monday

planSpec.domain: Jonas, a technical bootcamp instructor redesigning assessments
planSpec.audience: teachers moving from big exams to learning routines
planSpec.stakes: students can pass weekly projects while forgetting prior commands
planSpec.requiredBeat: he tells the cohort that every Monday quiz will include last month’s commands and asks them to explain one miss in a learning paragraph

examples.scenario: "Old material comes back Monday," Jonas says while a terminal prompt blinks on the projector. A student asks if the weekly quiz is punishment for forgetting commands from last month. Jonas points to the learning paragraph template beside the quiz. "One miss, explained and repaired," he says. Before the cohort starts, he must choose whether the quiz is a grade event or a scheduled return with reflection attached.
examples.whatToDo: Include old commands in Monday quizzes and require one learning paragraph that explains a miss, the repair, and when it returns.
examples.whyItMatters: Students can pass weekly projects while old commands fade. Scheduled retrieval plus reflection keeps prior material alive without turning the quiz into a trap.

examples.title: Chiara Rotates Insurance Cards at Lunch

planSpec.domain: Chiara, a small-business owner learning insurance licensing material
planSpec.stakes: licensing requires retrieval across products, regulations, and client scenarios
planSpec.requiredBeat: she builds a rotating box of product questions, client cases, and wrong-answer repairs for lunch breaks and Saturday review

examples.scenario: At 12:12 p.m., Chiara opens a shoe box of mixed client cards beside a wrong-answer sheet and half a sandwich. Product questions, regulation prompts, and client scenarios sit in the same stack. Each lunch break gives her ten cards; Saturday review gets only the misses. Before returning to the counter, Chiara must choose whether the wrong answers go back into the box with a repair date or disappear into another full reread.
examples.whatToDo: Rotate client cards at lunch, write misses on the wrong-answer sheet, and use Saturday for repaired retrieval instead of another full reread.
examples.whyItMatters: Licensing requires choosing across products, rules, and client facts. The mixed box keeps retrieval and repair moving inside a crowded workweek.

examples.title: Lin Redesigns Cross-Training After One Fault Stalls

planSpec.domain: Lin, a maintenance supervisor building cross-training for technicians
planSpec.audience: operations leaders applying the whole learning system
planSpec.stakes: technicians must diagnose unfamiliar faults when senior staff are away
planSpec.requiredBeat: the postmortem redesigns cross-training so each tech retrieves, simulates, rotates fault types, and repairs misses before certification

examples.scenario: What failed when the only trained technician was off shift? At 7:30 a.m. in the maintenance cage, Lin writes the question above a fault log, a rotation board, and a certification checklist. The postmortem shows attendance at the old workshop, but no one could diagnose the unfamiliar motor fault. Before signing the next checklist, Lin must choose between another workshop and a system of retrieval, rotating faults, repair notes, and delayed checks.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the one-time workshop with rotating fault simulations, closed-source retrieval, repair notes, and delayed certification checks.
examples.whyItMatters: Coverage depends on available skill, not attendance. Lin needs technicians who can retrieve and adapt when the senior expert is gone.

questions.prompt: A student has learned retrieval, spacing, interleaving, and calibration as separate tactics for final exams. What turns them into a system she can actually follow?
choices: A longer list of tips copied into a notebook
One final all-night review before the exam
A repeating schedule that retrieves, delays, mixes, checks, repairs, and returns to misses
questions.explanation: A system assigns each method a recurring job and gives misses a return date. Lists and last-minute review do not keep learning honest over time.

questions.prompt: A nurse-onboarding course teaches one topic per week, but floor handoffs mix medication safety, escalation, and patient education. Which redesign fits best?
choices: Keep clean weekly blocks because they are easier to schedule.
Cycle old topics into retrieval and mixed simulations across the month.
Remove simulations and rely on policy readings.
questions.explanation: The floor requires combined retrieval and selection. Mixed simulations with returning topics train transfer better than clean blocks or reading alone.

questions.prompt: An actor rereads two scripts straight through but may be called in for scenes out of order with only a few hours notice. What routine best prepares her?
choices: Read each script from page one every night until it feels familiar.
Memorize only the first scene because it starts the performance.
Record cue lines, cover her own lines, rotate scenes, and schedule missed entrances for delayed checks.
questions.explanation: Cue-based retrieval and interleaved scenes match the performance demand. Straight rereading can feel safe while leaving out-of-order entrances fragile.

questions.prompt: A bootcamp instructor sees students pass weekly projects and forget prior commands when new projects begin. Which assessment routine best supports durable learning?
choices: A big final exam with no prior checks
Monday quizzes that include older commands plus a learning paragraph on one miss
Only current-week project grades so students can focus
questions.explanation: Older-command retrieval fights forgetting, and the learning paragraph turns a miss into repair. Current-only grading lets prior knowledge fade unseen.

questions.prompt: A small-business owner studying for insurance licensing has only lunch breaks, Saturdays, and a box of mixed client cards. Which plan best combines the methods?
choices: Reread all notes every Saturday from the beginning.
Use mixed client cards at lunch, record misses, and use Saturday to retrieve repaired items.
Study only the product category she likes most first.
questions.explanation: The mixed card routine uses retrieval, interleaving, and repair inside limited time. Full rereads and preference-first study leave selection and weak spots underworked.

questions.prompt: A maintenance team attended a fault-diagnosis workshop, but only the senior technician can handle unfamiliar failures. What should the supervisor add before certification?
choices: Rotating fault simulations, closed-source retrieval, repair notes, and delayed checks
A signed attendance sheet for the original workshop
A longer slide deck with every possible fault listed
questions.explanation: Certification should require available skill: retrieve, diagnose, repair, and return after delay. Attendance and slides do not prove technicians can act.

questions.prompt: A student says she already uses retrieval for vocabulary, so spacing and interleaving are unnecessary for the course. What is the best response?
choices: Retrieval is stronger inside a loop that returns after delay and mixes cases for selection.
One good method should replace every other method.
Interleaving only matters for athletes, not students.
questions.explanation: Retrieval answers one problem, but spacing and interleaving add recovery and selection. The methods reinforce each other instead of competing for one slot.

questions.prompt: A teacher wants high-structure classes but worries structure will make students passive during biology units. Which design avoids that problem?
choices: Visible standards plus frequent retrieval, reflection, and repair of misses
More lectures with fewer checks so students feel trusted
Detailed answer keys with no student explanation required
questions.explanation: Structure supports active work when students retrieve, compare answers to standards, reflect, and repair. Structure without student production can become passive.

questions.prompt: A learner keeps a wrong-answer list beside the desk but never revisits it after the quiz is over. Which missing part prevents the list from improving learning?
choices: A scheduled return that requires retrieval of the repaired item
A more colorful notebook for the list
A rule that wrong answers should be forgotten immediately
questions.explanation: The wrong-answer list becomes useful when misses return for retrieval. Without a scheduled return, it records weakness without repairing it.

reviewCards.front: What turns separate study tactics into a learning system?
reviewCards.back: A recurring loop: retrieve, space, mix, check confidence, repair misses, and return to them after delay.

reviewCards.front: Why does a wrong-answer list need a return date?
reviewCards.back: A list only records the gap. A return date forces repaired retrieval, which is where the gap starts closing.

reviewCards.front: How should a trainer redesign one-topic-per-week onboarding?
reviewCards.back: Cycle topics back through retrieval and mixed simulations so learners practice the combinations they will face in real work.

reviewCards.front: What does a learning paragraph add after a quiz miss?
reviewCards.back: It makes the learner explain what failed, how it was repaired, and when it will return. The miss becomes a plan instead of a score.

reviewCards.front: A week is crowded. What smallest loop can still make learning stick?
reviewCards.back: One retrieval slot, one delayed review, one mixed set, one calibration check, and one repair block repeated every week.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is building a repeatable architecture for learning. Each method gets a job in the week: retrieve, delay, mix, check, repair, and return.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a course calendar is organized only by topic, then add weekly returns to old material and a Friday repair list.
If quizzes feel like one-off scores, then add a learning paragraph and a scheduled retry of missed ideas.
If onboarding is blocked by topic, then cycle old topics through mixed simulations before certification.
If study time is scattered, then use a small mixed card box and reserve one weekly block for repaired misses.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Create a seven-day loop with one retrieval slot, one delayed review, one mixed set, one calibration check, and one repair block. Put actual material into each slot.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Review the loop every Friday. Move misses into next week, retire items that survive delayed retrieval, and add one mixed case that forces selection.
